title: Contribution
lead: Make a useful contribution for future iGEM teams and document it on this page.
html:
Bronze Medal Criterion #3

Make a useful contribution for future iGEM teams and document it on this page.

Visit the Medals page for more information.

What Should this Page Contain?

Teams must document their contribution and explain why their effort is a contribution to fellow iGEMers. There is no single definition of what a contribution should be. We invite teams to be creative and generous in the knowledge, data or tools they may provide to the community.

A few examples of contributions are:

  • Creating a new BioBrick part or significantly improving an existing one in the iGEM Registry.
  • Developing software, tools, or resources that can considerably assist future iGEM teams.
  • Sharing optimized protocols, experimental techniques, or methodologies.
  • Any other contributions that provide a clear benefit to future iGEM teams.

Molecular Dynamics Simulation Workflow and Practical Know-how In this project, we used molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to evaluate the structural stability of the CoilE–CoilR coiled-coil and to compare linker designs connecting the coiled-coils to membrane proteins. GROMACS 2025.3 was mainly used for energy minimization, equilibration, production MD, and trajectory analysis. For membrane-containing systems, CHARMM-GUI was used to construct the membrane environment and generate the initial simulation files. The isolated CoilE–CoilR system was simulated using the AMBER99SB-ILDN force field with the TIP3P water model, while membrane-containing systems were prepared using the CHARMM force field provided through CHARMM-GUI.

One of the major challenges was preparing realistic initial structures for membrane simulations. In some cases, the predicted protein structures could not be placed appropriately within the membrane or caused unfavorable overlaps with the membrane components. We therefore used UCSF ChimeraX to inspect and manually adjust the orientation and geometry of the protein structures before constructing the final simulation systems. Rather than simply translating or stretching the proteins, we tried to preserve the original secondary structures and protein geometry as much as possible while modifying flexible regions or relative orientations so that the membrane proteins and coiled-coils could be arranged in physically reasonable positions. Also, the simulation environment was designed based on experimental and literature information. Membrane lipid composition, ionic conditions, pH-related assumptions, intermolecular interactions between CoilE and CoilR were selected with reference to previous studies.

We also established a practical workflow for trajectory analysis. After production MD, trajectories were fitted using the CoilE–CoilR backbone to remove overall translation and rotation, and structural properties such as RMSD, RMSF, inter-coil distance, radius of gyration, solvent-accessible surface area, and interaction-related parameters were analyzed. Custom index groups were created with gmx make_ndx so that the CoilE and CoilR regions could be analyzed independently from the membrane proteins, lipids, water, and ions. When residue numbers were duplicated between different protein chains, we found that using residue indices (ri) rather than residue numbers (r) was useful for selecting the intended region without accidentally including residues from another chain.

Moreover, when constructing the full membrane-containing system, initially, we attempted to combine both the TM-side membrane system and the Intimin-side outer-membrane system in CHARMM-GUI. However, handling both membrane systems simultaneously required a large amount of computational processing and resulted in very long setup times. To make the workflow more practical, we changed the construction strategy: the Intimin-side membrane system was prepared first, while the TM-side component was introduced without its membrane and the inner membrane was constructed afterward around the TM protein. This stepwise assembly significantly reduced the computational burden and allowed the system construction to proceed successfully.

Another important point was the preparation of structures for umbrella sampling. Initially, we attempted to generate sampling configurations by pulling CoilE and CoilR apart from an associated structure. However, this approach did not produce suitable configurations for our system. We therefore changed the strategy and started from separated CoilE and CoilR structures, gradually pulling them toward each other instead. Structures at different inter-coil distances were then extracted and used as initial configurations for umbrella sampling. This experience showed that the direction of the pulling simulation can strongly affect the quality of the generated sampling structures, and that reversing the pulling direction can be a practical solution when the conventional approach does not work well.

During the analysis, we also found that individual metrics should not be interpreted independently. For example, a lower RMSF does not necessarily mean that a linker is more suitable for coiled-coil-mediated adhesion. A linker must provide sufficient flexibility while maintaining a geometry that allows CoilE and CoilR to approach and interact. We therefore evaluated linker candidates using multiple criteria, including RMSF, structural changes, inter-coil distance, contact maintenance, and whether dissociation occurred during the simulation.

Through these processes, we developed not only an MD workflow for evaluating coiled-coil stability, but also practical strategies for constructing difficult membrane-protein systems, preparing umbrella-sampling configurations, troubleshooting structural problems, and translating simulation results into design criteria for Wet Lab experiments. We hope that these approaches can serve as useful references for future iGEM teams performing MD simulations of membrane proteins, linkers, or protein–protein interactions.
